summary: Defines OAM messages for MPLS-based transport networks that tell an endpoint about conditions that disrupt service. It creates an OAM channel and messages that signal different failure types. It was later updated by RFC 7214.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6427 defines MPLS messages that report faults and administrative locks to the endpoints of affected paths. The messages help those endpoints suppress secondary alarms and, when a server failure is confirmed, may support faster recovery.

what is the l-flag in mpls fault oam
subtitle: In-band MPLS messages that tell service endpoints about faults and administrative locks.

tldr.problem: A fault in a lower network layer can disrupt many client paths and cause a burst of alarms that hide the original problem.
tldr.mechanism: Intermediate nodes send Alarm Indication Signal or Lock Report messages downstream over a dedicated MPLS fault-management channel, repeating them until the condition clears.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can distinguish a fault from an administrative lock, suppress related alarms and use a link-down indication where appropriate. RFC 6427 was updated by RFC 7214.

today: RFC 6427 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2011. It has been updated by RFC 7214.

sections.title: Why Fault Messages Are Needed
sections.content:
When a lower, or server, layer fails, every client path using it may be disrupted. Those clients could each report an alarm, obscuring the underlying fault. RFC 6427 defines Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM) messages that carry a disruptive condition to affected client endpoints.

The messages are intended for MPLS Transport Profile LSPs. Intermediate nodes insert them into affected client paths downstream of the fault and continue sending them until the condition clears.
sections.plainLanguage: A failure in one layer can disrupt many paths above it. A message about the lower-layer condition helps those paths avoid reporting only separate symptoms.

sections.title: Faults, Locks and Two Message Types
sections.content:
A fault is a function's inability to perform a required action, excluding planned work and lack of external resources. A lock is an administrative state where only test traffic and OAM dedicated to the LSP are expected. A server failure means the fault has lasted long enough that the server layer is considered to have stopped providing its service.

An Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) reports a fault. A Lock Report (LKR) reports an administrative lock. Both can suppress alarms in the layer above. A receiver may treat an AIS with the Link Down flag set, or an LKR, as loss of continuity at the client layer.
sections.plainLanguage: AIS reports that a fault has occurred; LKR reports that an administrator locked the layer. The distinction lets the receiving endpoint respond to the right kind of condition.

sections.title: When the Link Down Flag Is Set
sections.content:
The L-Flag in an AIS message carries a Link Down Indication. A node must not set it until it determines that the fault is a server failure, and it must set it once that determination is made. During a protection switch, the flag stays clear until the expected repair time passes without restoring the link.

Endpoints may use a set flag as a continuity failure. If their continuity checks already run quickly, they may use AIS only to suppress alarms. In slower-checking environments, the indication can support faster switch-over.
sections.plainLanguage: The L-Flag means the server layer has failed, not merely that protection is switching. A receiver may use it to treat the client path as down.

sections.title: The Fault Channel and Message Fields
sections.content:
Fault messages travel in-band in a client LSP or multi-segment pseudowire, after an Associated Channel Header. The channel type is 0x0058. This channel does not use an Associated Channel TLV header.

The message contains a version, reserved field, message type, flags, Refresh Timer, total TLV length and optional TLVs. Message type 1 is AIS and type 2 is LKR. The timer gives the maximum number of seconds between messages and ranges from 1 to 20. The R-Flag indicates that a previously reported condition has been removed. Defined TLVs can carry an interface identifier or a global identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The message identifies an alarm or lock, carries status flags, and says how often it will be repeated. A dedicated channel type keeps it distinguishable from other associated-channel traffic.

sections.title: Sending, Refreshing and Clearing Messages
sections.content:
A sender repeats a message two more times at one-second intervals, then uses the Refresh Timer until the condition clears. The timer must stay the same for messages about that incident. If the sender stops without an explicit clear message, the receiver clears the condition after 3.5 times the timer.

To clear a condition sooner, a sender may set the R-Flag and send the message immediately and twice more at one-second intervals. At minimum, implementations must send AIS and LKR once per second, set the L-Flag for a server failure, and receive messages with any allowed timer.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages repeat while a condition remains. A receiver expires a condition after missed refreshes, or clears it sooner when it receives an explicit removal message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The fault messages depend on the security of the Generic Associated Channel. A specific concern is that this channel can provide a covert path between endpoints, so transit nodes should not police it.

False fault messages could cause denial of service. The RFC says an attacker would generally need access to a node providing the service. Where external MPLS traffic could introduce a GAL followed by a fault message, operators should filter messages with the GAL at the top of the label stack.
sections.plainLanguage: False alarm messages could disrupt service, and the channel has security limits. The RFC recommends filtering a specific kind of message that could enter from external MPLS traffic.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Version number; the current value is 1.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Sent as zero and ignored when received.

fields.name: Refresh Timer
fields.desc: Maximum seconds between messages; allowed values are 1 to 20.

fields.name: Total TLV Length
fields.desc: Total length in bytes of included TLVs.

items.label: AIS
items.desc: Reports a fault detected in the server layer.
